blocks.title: Listening Part 1
blocks.mode: Fresh classroom check: one play, no pausing, no support
blocks.instructions: Complete the form. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

stimulus.title: Recording IELTS-21-L1 transcript (teacher-private)
paragraphs: CLERK: Greenway Community Centre, bookings. How can I help?
DANIELA: Hello. I'd like to book a room for my daughter's eighteenth birthday party.
CLERK: Of course. What date were you thinking of?
DANIELA: Friday the twelfth of July, if possible.
CLERK: Let me check. I'm afraid Friday the twelfth is already taken. The day after is free, though.
DANIELA: The thirteenth? That's fine, actually. Let's say Saturday.
CLERK: And how many guests are you expecting?
DANIELA: We first said sixty, but we've cut the list, so around forty-five.
CLERK: In that case, the Main Hall would be too big. I'd suggest the Garden Room. It holds up to fifty and opens onto the garden.
DANIELA: That sounds lovely. What time could we have it from?
CLERK: What time would you like?
DANIELA: Guests will arrive at seven, but we'll need to decorate first, so could we have the room from half past five?
CLERK: Yes, that's fine. The Garden Room is thirty-two pounds an hour in the evening. During the day it's twenty-five.
DANIELA: OK. Is there a deposit?
CLERK: Yes, fifty pounds, which we return after the event if there's no damage.
DANIELA: Do you provide tables and chairs?
CLERK: Tables, chairs and a sound system are all included. You'll need to bring your own tablecloths, though.
DANIELA: And is there parking?
CLERK: There's no parking at the front, but you can use the car park behind the library, which is free after six.
CLERK: Could I take your name?
DANIELA: Daniela Moretti. That's M, O, R, E, T, T, I.
CLERK: Thank you. And on the day, please collect the keys from the café next door, because our office closes at five.

blocks.title: Reading Passage 1
blocks.mode: Fresh classroom check: twenty minutes, no dictionary, no support
blocks.instructions: Questions 11-14: which paragraph, A-F, contains the following information? Questions 15-19: write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Questions 20-23: choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

stimulus.title: The teenage clock
paragraphs: Over the past two decades, a growing number of cities have committed themselves to ambitious programmes of tree planting, frequently pledging to plant hundreds of thousands or even millions of trees within a decade. Urban trees were once regarded primarily as decoration, valued for softening the appearance of streets and parks but seldom considered essential infrastructure. That perception has altered considerably as researchers have accumulated evidence that trees perform a range of measurable services, from moderating temperatures to reducing the volume of water that flows into drains after heavy rain. Municipal budgets that once treated tree maintenance as a minor expense are now beginning to allocate funding comparable to that given to roads and lighting.

The most frequently cited benefit concerns heat. Densely built urban areas are typically several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect, because asphalt, brick and concrete absorb solar energy during the day and release it slowly after dark. Trees counteract this in two ways: their canopies shade the surfaces beneath them, and they release water vapour through their leaves, a process that cools the surrounding air. Measurements taken on hot afternoons have found that streets lined with mature trees can be considerably cooler at pavement level than comparable streets without them, a difference that may be significant for elderly residents and others vulnerable to heat-related illness. The cooling effect depends heavily on the size of the canopy, however, so newly planted saplings provide relatively little benefit for many years until they reach maturity.

Trees also influence the movement of water. When rain falls on paved surfaces, it runs off rapidly into drainage systems, which can be overwhelmed during intense storms, causing localised flooding. A tree canopy intercepts a proportion of the rainfall, some of which evaporates before reaching the ground, while roots improve the capacity of the soil to absorb water. Several cities now incorporate tree pits and planted strips into their drainage plans, although engineers emphasise that trees can supplement, but not replace, conventional drainage infrastructure. The effect is greatest during moderate rainfall; in the most extreme storms, the soil quickly becomes saturated and the contribution of trees becomes comparatively small.

Claims regarding air quality are more complicated. Leaves can capture fine particles from the air, and many planting schemes are promoted on the grounds that they will make the air healthier to breathe. However, the overall effect at city scale appears to be modest, and in narrow streets enclosed by tall buildings, a dense canopy can actually trap vehicle exhaust close to the ground by reducing the circulation of air. Some species also release natural compounds that contribute to the formation of ground-level ozone in hot weather. Researchers therefore recommend that species and locations be selected with care, rather than assuming that more trees will automatically improve the air. Pollen from certain species can also aggravate allergies, a consideration that planners have not always taken into account when selecting trees for streets near schools and hospitals.

Planting a tree, moreover, is considerably easier than ensuring that it survives. Young trees in cities face compacted soil, restricted root space, damage from vehicles and vandalism, and, in many regions, increasingly frequent summer droughts. Studies in several countries have reported that a substantial proportion of newly planted street trees die within their first few years, often because watering is neglected once the initial planting has been completed. As a result, some urban foresters argue that targets based on the number of trees planted are misleading, and that cities should instead measure the extent of canopy cover that is actually maintained over time. Some cities now employ teams responsible solely for caring for young trees during their first three summers, and report markedly higher survival rates as a result.

There are also questions of fairness. In many cities, tree cover is unevenly distributed, with wealthier neighbourhoods enjoying considerably more shade than poorer ones, which are frequently those most exposed to heat and pollution. A number of local authorities have consequently begun to direct new planting towards areas with the least existing cover. Even this approach has generated debate, however, since residents in some districts have expressed concern that improvements to the local environment could increase property prices and rents, eventually displacing the very people the programmes were intended to benefit.

B  They clean city air more than any other measure.

C  to compare tree planting in different countries

stages.title: Transfer Listening answers
stages.student: Transfer answers 1-10 to the answer grid in two minutes.

stages.title: Reading passage: twenty minutes plus transfer

stages.say: Ten minutes left... two minutes left: no blanks.

stages.title: Review: Listening and Reading answers

stages.check: Each learner has recorded scores and conditions.

blocks.title: Plants in the office
blocks.instructions: Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

stimulus.title: Plants in the office
paragraphs: Many companies now place plants in offices, hoping to make workplaces more pleasant. Some studies have reported that employees in offices with plants say they feel more satisfied with their surroundings.

Claims that a few pot plants can significantly clean the air in a whole building, however, are treated with caution by many scientists, because laboratory tests in sealed chambers do not reflect conditions in a ventilated office.
Plants also need care. Without regular watering and enough light, they quickly look unhealthy, and a row of dying plants may do more harm than good to the atmosphere of an office.

items.prompt: Some employees report greater satisfaction with offices that contain plants.
items.evidence: employees in offices with plants say they feel more satisfied with their surroundings

items.prompt: Scientists agree that a few plants can clean the air of an entire building.
items.evidence: are treated with caution by many scientists
items.reason: Scientists are cautious, not in agreement with the claim.

items.prompt: Office plants are more expensive to maintain than air filters.
items.evidence: No cost comparison.

items.prompt: Poorly maintained plants may make an office feel worse.
items.evidence: may do more harm than good to the atmosphere of an office
